stem: Based on the text, Okafor would most likely agree with which statement about lake-effect snow?
stimulus: Forecasters have long relied on a simple rule for lake-effect snow: heavy bands form only when the air passing over a lake is at least 13°C colder than the water's surface. Meteorologist Lena Okafor, however, argues that this rule leaves out wind direction. When wind blows along a lake's full length, the air gathers heat and moisture over a much longer stretch of water. Okafor's records show that such winds have produced heavy snow even when the temperature gap was only 8°C.
choices: Heavy lake-effect snow forms only when the air is at least 13°C colder than the lake.
Heavy snow can form with a small temperature gap if wind crosses the lake's full length.
The temperature gap between air and water has no effect on whether snow bands form.
Wind direction matters less to lake-effect snow than forecasters have usually assumed.
explanation: After 'however,' the passage gives Okafor's claim: wind blowing along a lake's full length can produce heavy snow even with an 8°C gap, well under the 13°C rule. Choice B applies that claim directly.

A.why: This is the forecasters' rule that Okafor is arguing against. You picked the view the passage explains first instead of the one that comes after 'however.'

C.why: Okafor says the rule is incomplete, not that temperature doesn't matter. You took her point further than she does.

D.why: This reverses Okafor's view. She argues that wind direction matters more than the traditional rule allows.

stem: Based on the text, Reyes would most likely agree with which statement about a city that wants more people walking along a shopping street?
stimulus: Many cities widen sidewalks to bring more pedestrians to their shopping districts. Urban planner Tomás Reyes argues that width is not what keeps people walking. What matters, he says, is how often a walker passes a new doorway. In his counts across twelve neighborhoods, narrow sidewalks lined with many small shops drew more foot traffic than wide sidewalks running past long, windowless store walls.
choices: Widening the sidewalks would be the most reliable way to draw more pedestrians.
Narrowing the sidewalks would draw more pedestrians than any other change.
A few large stores with wide entrances would draw the most pedestrians.
Adding many small shopfronts would likely do more than widening the sidewalks.
explanation: Reyes says foot traffic depends on how often walkers pass a new doorway, and his counts favored streets with many small shops. For a city that wants more walkers, his reasoning points to more shopfronts, not wider pavement.

A.why: This is the common practice Reyes argues against. You picked the view the passage opens with instead of his claim.

B.why: Reyes says width isn't the deciding factor. He never says narrow sidewalks are better, so you pushed his point too far.

C.why: A few large stores means fewer doorways. Reyes's reasoning predicts that would draw fewer walkers, not more.

stem: Based on the text, Lindqvist would most likely agree with which statement about the search for planets that could support life?
stimulus: Most searches for life-supporting planets focus on worlds orbiting stars like the Sun, the one star known to host life. Astronomer Hana Lindqvist argues that this focus may be too narrow. Orange dwarf stars, which are slightly smaller and cooler than the Sun, stay stable for billions of years longer and give off fewer harmful bursts of radiation. Those traits, she suggests, could give life on a nearby planet more time and safer conditions in which to develop.
choices: Searches should give more attention to planets that orbit orange dwarf stars.
Searches should concentrate mainly on planets that orbit stars like the Sun.
Planets that orbit stars like the Sun are unable to support any form of life.
Orange dwarf stars burn out too quickly for life on their planets to develop.
explanation: Lindqvist calls the Sun-focused search 'too narrow' and explains why orange dwarfs may be good hosts for life. It follows that she would want searches to pay more attention to planets around those stars.

B.why: This is the usual search strategy that Lindqvist says is too narrow. You picked the view she is arguing against.

C.why: Lindqvist wants the search widened, not Sun-like stars ruled out. The passage itself notes that one Sun-like star does host life.

D.why: The passage says orange dwarfs stay stable for billions of years longer than the Sun. This choice reverses that.

stem: Based on the text, Abernathy would most likely agree with which statement about the rise of flowering plants?
stimulus: Textbooks often describe flowering plants as sweeping across the Cretaceous landscape and quickly crowding out conifers. Paleobotanist Ruth Abernathy questions that picture. In layers of fossil pollen from a Montana lake bed, she found that conifer pollen remained far more abundant for roughly ten million years after flowering-plant pollen first appeared. Abernathy concludes that flowering plants likely gained ground gradually, over a span much longer than the textbook account allows.
choices: Flowering plants took over from conifers rapidly once they first appeared.
Flowering plants never became more common than conifers in any region.
Flowering plants displaced conifers more slowly than is commonly claimed.
Conifers appeared in the fossil record later than flowering plants did.
explanation: Abernathy's pollen record shows conifers stayed dominant for about ten million years after flowering plants appeared, and she concludes that flowering plants gained ground gradually. That matches a slower takeover than the textbook version.

A.why: This is the textbook picture that Abernathy questions. You picked the view the passage sets up before her evidence.

B.why: Abernathy says flowering plants gained ground slowly, not that they never did. Her evidence comes from one site, so 'any region' goes far beyond it.

D.why: The passage describes conifers as already established when flowering-plant pollen first shows up. This choice reverses the order.

stem: Based on the text, Moreau would most likely agree with which statement about the line between languages and dialects?
stimulus: In principle, linguists separate languages from dialects with one test: if speakers of two varieties can understand each other, they speak dialects of a single language. Linguist Inès Moreau argues that in practice the line is often drawn by politics. Some varieties that are officially counted as separate languages are easy for each other's speakers to understand. Meanwhile, some varieties grouped as dialects of one national language are not. To Moreau, the distinction is less purely linguistic than it seems.
choices: Two varieties are separate languages whenever their speakers cannot understand each other.
How varieties are labeled often reflects politics as well as whether speakers understand each other.
Speech varieties are so alike that they cannot be meaningfully grouped or classified at all.
Political boundaries have little influence on how speech varieties come to be labeled.
explanation: Moreau says the line is 'often drawn by politics' and is 'less purely linguistic than it seems.' That means labels reflect politics as well as whether speakers understand each other, which is what B says.

A.why: This is the textbook test that Moreau says often fails in practice. You picked the view the passage explains first instead of her argument.

C.why: Moreau says the distinction is less purely linguistic, not that classification is impossible. You pushed 'less clear-cut' all the way to 'can't be done.'

D.why: This reverses Moreau's central claim, which is that politics often shapes the labels.

stem: Based on the text, Brandauer would most likely agree with which statement about the waltz's popularity in the 1800s?
stimulus: Historians usually credit the waltz's rapid spread across nineteenth-century Europe to the grand public ballrooms of Vienna, where orchestras played it nightly. Musicologist Ilse Brandauer, however, points to sales records from music publishers. Cheap printed arrangements of waltzes for piano sold by the hundreds of thousands, she notes, so many families were playing and dancing the waltz at home long before they ever entered a ballroom.
choices: It came mainly from orchestras performing in Vienna's public ballrooms.
It owed more to music played in private homes than is usually recognized.
It had nothing at all to do with performances in public ballrooms.
It depended mostly on the skill of professional concert pianists.
explanation: Brandauer's claim comes after 'however': sheet music sold for home pianos let families play and dance the waltz before they went to ballrooms. So she would say private homes mattered more than historians usually admit, which is choice B.

A.why: This is the usual view that Brandauer argues against. You picked the explanation the passage lays out first, not the one Brandauer actually holds.

C.why: Brandauer says home playing mattered more than people think. She never says ballrooms played no part. You took her position too far.

D.why: The passage is about ordinary families playing cheap arrangements at home, not professional pianists. You latched onto the word 'piano' and missed her point.

stem: Based on the text, Reyes-Aldana would most likely agree with which statement about urban legends and folktales?
stimulus: Folklorists have traditionally placed urban legends and folktales in separate categories: urban legends are modern stories that tellers claim are true, while folktales are old stories understood as fiction. Folklorist Tomás Reyes-Aldana challenges this division. Many urban legends, he observes, reuse the plots of centuries-old tales almost exactly, changing only surface details, so that a haunted carriage becomes a haunted car.
choices: They belong in separate categories because one is modern and the other is old.
They cannot be told apart from each other in any way at all.
They are most often set in cars and other modern vehicles.
They are more closely related than the usual division suggests.
explanation: Reyes-Aldana challenges the separation by showing that urban legends reuse old folktale plots and change only surface details. That points to a closer relationship than the traditional categories allow, which is choice D.

A.why: This is the traditional division that Reyes-Aldana challenges. You picked it because the passage explains it clearly in the first sentence.

B.why: He says the two share plots. He doesn't say every difference disappears. You pushed 'closely related' all the way to 'identical'.

C.why: The car is just one example of a changed surface detail. You took an incidental example for his argument.

stem: Based on the text, Ramanathan would most likely agree with which statement about judging a wetland's health?
stimulus: Conservation managers usually judge a wetland's health by counting the species of birds and fish that live there. Ecologist Priya Ramanathan contends that these counts overlook the soil microbes that break down waste and hold nutrients in place. In the wetlands she has studied, microbe populations collapsed years before any decline in the larger animals appeared.
choices: Examining soil microbes can reveal problems that animal counts may miss.
Counting bird and fish species is the most reliable way to judge it.
Counting animal species provides no useful information about it.
Microbe losses usually follow a decline in the larger animals.
explanation: Ramanathan says animal counts overlook soil microbes, and that microbes collapsed years before the animals declined. So checking the microbes can catch trouble that animal counts would miss, which is choice A.

B.why: This is the managers' usual method, the one Ramanathan argues is incomplete. You took the view she's arguing against as her own.

C.why: She says animal counts miss something, not that they're useless. You went from 'incomplete' to 'worthless'.

D.why: The passage says the microbes collapsed years before the animals declined. You reversed the order.

stem: Based on the text, Okafor would most likely agree with which statement about how songbirds choose nest sites?
stimulus: Researchers have generally assumed that songbirds choose nest sites mainly to stay hidden from predators. Ornithologist Daniel Okafor, however, found that the house wrens he observed in Oregon repeatedly chose spots that caught the morning sun, even when those spots were more exposed. The added warmth, he reports, helped the eggs develop faster.
choices: Birds choose nest sites mainly so they can stay hidden from predators.
Predators have no effect on where any songbird builds its nest.
Factors besides hiding from predators can strongly influence the choice.
Wrens avoid sunny sites because the exposure puts their eggs at risk.
explanation: Okafor's wrens chose sunny, more exposed spots because warmth helped the eggs. That shows something other than hiding, here warmth, can drive where birds nest, which is choice C.

A.why: This is the general assumption that comes before 'however'. You picked the view Okafor's findings push against.

B.why: Okafor shows that warmth also matters. He doesn't show predators don't matter, and he studied one species, not 'any songbird'.

D.why: The wrens chose sunny sites, and the sun helped the eggs. This choice reverses what the passage says.

stem: Based on the text, Zhao would most likely agree with which statement about dating the first flowering plants?
stimulus: Paleobotanists have usually dated the first flowering plants by their oldest fossil flowers, which are about 130 million years old. Paleobotanist Mei-Lin Zhao argues that this method may set the date too late. Pollen grains survive as fossils far more readily than delicate petals do, she notes, and some fossil pollen suggests that flowering plants appeared several million years earlier.
choices: The oldest fossil flowers show when flowering plants first appeared.
Fossil pollen may give a better estimate than fossil flowers do.
Fossil flowers are useless for studying the history of plants.
Petals survive as fossils more readily than pollen grains do.
explanation: Zhao argues that dating by fossil flowers may set the date too late. Pollen fossilizes more readily, and some pollen points to an earlier start. So she would favor pollen as the better guide to when flowering plants first appeared, which is choice B.

A.why: This is the usual dating method that Zhao says may set the date too late. You picked the view the passage explains first.

C.why: Zhao says flower fossils may give too late a date. She doesn't say they're useless for all study of plant history. You pushed her claim too far.

D.why: The passage says pollen survives more readily than petals. This choice reverses that comparison.
